Chapter 6. The Heart of Intention—Why Actions Begin Within.
Picture this—there’s always that quiet moment before you do something. Maybe it’s just a split second, so quick you might not even notice it. But in that pause, you decide why you’re about to act.
Think about a teacher staying late to help a student. Is it for a thank you? Or just because they care? Or maybe a neighbor gives to charity—are they looking for a pat on the back, or are they simply trying to make a difference?
It’s in these tiny, almost hidden spaces that what we do gets its true meaning.
Sunan Abu Dawud brings us back to this inner world over and over again. The traditions remind us: the value of what we do really starts with intention. It’s not just about what you do—but why you do it. The Prophet’s words ring out: “Actions are judged by intentions.” You’ve probably heard that saying before, maybe at home or in class. It’s shaped how so many people approach faith—and even the simple things in life.
There’s a story I love: a man travels a long way to join the Prophet’s community. Some folks said he came for faith. Others whispered it was all about marrying someone. But the Prophet—always gentle, always wise—explains, everyone gets what their heart truly wants. Even if two people do the exact same thing, the meaning behind it can be completely different, depending on what’s in their heart.
Focusing on intention brings a special kind of honesty to faith. It’s easy to just go through the motions—praying, helping out, doing good—because that’s what’s expected. But these traditions invite us to pause. To check in with ourselves for a moment before each prayer, each act of kindness, each word we say. Most of the time, we don’t even realize how quickly our intentions can wander... or how simple it is to bring them back, just by reflecting for a second.
And if you ever struggle with doubts, or find your mind drifting? You’re not alone. The traditions offer real comfort here. Sincerity isn’t about being perfect—it’s about coming back, again and again, to remember why you’re doing what you do. Even if you mess up, making the effort to realign your intention is itself a kind of faith.
Over time, this practice doesn’t just change what you do—it slowly shapes the person you become.
